title: Yara and the Room
premise: Folklorist Theo Kavanagh arrives in the drowned valley village of Hollowmere to record songs that locals refuse to sing twice, and discovers a parish register listing a bell that was melted down in 1911 — yet still rings each night at the hour of an old drowning. The ringing is an inheritance: every generation, one villager is 'invited in' to pay for a century-old injustice, and this year the room beneath the church has chosen Theo, whose grandmother fled the village carrying the deed that should have saved her sister. To survive until sunrise, Theo must learn the true song, return what was stolen, and name the guilty dead aloud — trading their inherited identity as outsider for a place among the remembered. The book ends with the bell falling silent forever and Theo choosing to stay, keeper now of songs sung only once.
about_author: Felix Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist from the Ardennes who spent a decade cataloguing parish records in depopulated French villages before turning to fiction. Their work blends documentary precision with folk horror, and they claim never to write about a place they haven't slept in overnight.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Theo Kavanagh arrives in Hollowmere by bus, tape recorder in hand, and coaxes a fragmentary drowning-ballad from old Marta Voss — who stops mid-verse, pale, refusing to continue. POV: Theo. Beat: curiosity curdling into unease as three villagers leave the pub rather than hear the second half.

chapters.title: A Register of Missing Things
chapters.summary: In the vestry archive, Theo finds the 1911 inventory: the great bell sold for scrap, and beside it a page torn out. The vicar, Reverend Ilse Brandt, watches them too closely. POV: Theo. Beat: scholarly excitement shadowed by the sense of being expected.

chapters.title: The Hour That Isn't on Any Clock
chapters.summary: At 3:07 a.m., a bell tolls though no bell exists; Theo films it, hears it through walls, through teeth. In the morning, villagers deny everything with practiced ease. POV: Theo. Beat: rational certainty beginning to crack against unanimous denial.

chapters.title: Marta's Second Verse
chapters.summary: Marta, drunk and frightened, sings the forbidden continuation: a girl drowned in the flooded quarry in 1911 while the village rang the bell to drown her cries. She names Theo's grandmother. POV: Theo. Beat: personal history detonating inside folklore.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Took
chapters.summary: Among Theo's mother's papers: a deed and letters proving the drowned girl, Lena, was cheated of the cottage that would have been her refuge — and that Theo's family profited. POV: Theo, interleaved with 1911 letters. Beat: guilt arriving as inheritance.

chapters.title: The Room Beneath
chapters.summary: Theo finds the bricked hatch under the church floor, warm to the touch, breathing faintly. Inside, something answers when they speak their own name. POV: Theo. Beat: dread made intimate and architectural.

chapters.title: The Village That Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Ilse finally talks: the ringing is the village's bargain — one invited per generation, chosen by blood-debt, so the rest may live unhaunted. This year the debt is Theo's. POV: Ilse. Beat: horror reframed as civic complicity.

chapters.title: Doors That Have Decided
chapters.summary: Theo tries to leave; the road loops back to Hollowmere no matter which way they drive. Phones show the village on no map. POV: Theo. Beat: panic, then the cold realization that leaving was never offered.

chapters.title: The Choir of the Guilty
chapters.summary: At nightfall the dead assemble in the churchyard — the 1911 congregation, faces like wet photographs — singing the ballad complete, waiting for Theo's verse. POV: Theo. Beat: awe weaponized into terror.

chapters.title: Marta's Confession
chapters.summary: Dying Marta admits her father helped hold Lena under; she has sung the first verse nightly for sixty years as penance. She gives Theo the torn register page. POV: Marta, then Theo. Beat: grief and fury braided together.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: The page lists not the bell's sale but its true fate: never melted — sunk in the quarry with Lena, ringing underwater ever since. The bell is her coffin lid. POV: Theo. Beat: understanding as a new kind of horror.

chapters.title: They Offer a Substitute
chapters.summary: The village proposes a way out: bring someone else — a drifter, a child of another debtless line — and the room will take them instead. POV: Theo. Beat: temptation, and Theo's refusal that costs them the village's last protection.

chapters.title: Excommunicated by Consent
chapters.summary: Refusing the substitute, Theo is shut out of every house; even Ilse bars the vicarage door. The night comes early, the sun failing at noon. POV: Theo. Beat: isolation absolute, resolve hardening.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: In the church alone, Theo reads the rite backwards and learns the truth: the village didn't trap the dead — it invited the bell's hunger in, in 1911, to silence Lena permanently. Every ringing since is the invitation renewing itself. POV: Theo. Beat: the horror's logic fully revealed.

chapters.title: Lena
chapters.summary: The drowned girl appears — not monstrous but patient, waterlogged, holding out her hand for the deed. She doesn't want Theo's life; she wants her name restored and her thief's line ended or redeemed. POV: Theo. Beat: terror softening into terrible empathy.

chapters.title: The Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Theo understands no court can touch men eighty years dead, and the living will never confess. Justice must be enacted, not petitioned: the song must be sung whole, in the church, by a Kavanagh, naming every guilty name. POV: Theo. Beat: acceptance of terrible agency.

chapters.title: Rehearsal at Midnight
chapters.summary: With Marta's corpse cold in the pew behind them, Theo rehearses the full ballad, voice breaking on the verses that accuse their own blood. The bell rings along, learning them. POV: Theo. Beat: grim determination edged with self-erasure.

chapters.title: The Village Breaks
chapters.summary: Villagers storm the church to stop the singing — some to save themselves, one, young Piet, to help. In the struggle the floor hatch cracks open and the room exhales. POV: alternating Theo and Piet. Beat: chaos, betrayal, unexpected alliance.

chapters.title: The Whole Song
chapters.summary: Climax: bleeding, hoarse, Theo sings all eleven verses before the assembled dead, naming the guilty — including their grandmother — and lays the deed on the wet stone. The bell rises from the quarry, dripping, and hangs itself in the empty tower. POV: Theo. Beat: cathartic, sacrificial courage.

chapters.title: Sunrise Terms
chapters.summary: The dead wait on the verdict of the bell. It rings once — for Lena, free — and falls silent. But the room demands a keeper, someone who knows the song, or the invitation renews. POV: Theo. Beat: victory shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: Keeper of Songs Sung Once
chapters.summary: Theo sends the recordings away and stays, taking the cottage that should have been Lena's, teaching Piet the verses so the song will never again be sung twice by accident. POV: Theo. Beat: quiet, earned peace laced with permanent vigilance.

chapters.title: Coda: The Bell That Doesn't Ring
chapters.summary: Epilogue, months later: a folklorist's letter arrives asking about Hollowmere's famous silent bell. Theo writes back that there is no bell, no village worth visiting — and locks the church door as the floor breathes, contentedly, once. POV: Theo. Beat: resolution as ongoing guardianship, unease folded into home.
